title: APIs & Realtime
summary: How callers talk to you, and how you talk back. 7 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: WebSockets / Persistent Connections — A long-lived bidirectional connection, so the server can push without the client asking and latency is one hop rather than one poll interval.
Server-Sent Events — A one-way stream of events over a normal HTTP response, with browser-native reconnect and event ids for resumption.
REST — Resource-oriented HTTP with standard verbs, status codes and cacheable GETs — the default public API shape.
gRPC — Binary RPC over HTTP/2 with an IDL-defined contract, code generation, streaming and multiplexing.
GraphQL — A single endpoint where the client declares exactly which fields of a graph it wants, in one round trip.
Webhooks — Pushing events to a URL the customer registered, so their server learns about changes without polling yours.
Cursor Pagination — Returning a page plus an opaque cursor pointing at the last item, so the next page seeks rather than counting from the start.

questions.prompt: WebSockets / Persistent Connections vs Server-Sent Events vs Webhooks — what decides between them?
points: Server-Sent Events — Server-to-client only, over plain HTTP, with automatic browser reconnect. Usually enough for feeds and notifications.
Webhooks — When the recipient is a server rather than a browser, push to their endpoint instead of holding a socket.
WebSockets / Persistent Connections — A long-lived bidirectional connection, so the server can push without the client asking and latency is one hop rather than one poll interval.
questions.answer: Server-Sent Events: Server-to-client only, over plain HTTP, with automatic browser reconnect. Usually enough for feeds and notifications. Webhooks: When the recipient is a server rather than a browser, push to their endpoint instead of holding a socket.

questions.prompt: WebSockets / Persistent Connections appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Chat System — Holds the client connection so inbound messages are pushed instantly, with presence and delivery receipts riding the same channel.
Design a Ride-Sharing Service — Carries continuous driver location updates and ride-match offers — both server-initiated and both latency-critical.
Design a Collaborative Document Editor — Streams each operation to every other collaborator, which is the only way the shared-cursor experience can feel live.
Design a Live Streaming Service — Powers chat and reactions alongside the video, providing the interactive layer a segment-based CDN path structurally cannot.
questions.answer: WebSockets / Persistent Connections carries different work in each: in Design a Chat System, holds the client connection so inbound messages are pushed instantly, with presence and delivery receipts riding the same channel. in Design a Ride-Sharing Service, carries continuous driver location updates and ride-match offers — both server-initiated and both latency-critical. in Design a Collaborative Document Editor, streams each operation to every other collaborator, which is the only way the shared-cursor experience can feel live. in Design a Live Streaming Service, powers chat and reactions alongside the video, providing the interactive layer a segment-based CDN path structurally cannot.

questions.prompt: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL — what decides between them?
points: gRPC — Internal, high-volume, strongly-typed service calls where efficiency and contracts matter.
GraphQL — When clients need very different shapes of the same graph and round trips are the pain.
REST — Resource-oriented HTTP with standard verbs, status codes and cacheable GETs — the default public API shape.
questions.answer: gRPC: Internal, high-volume, strongly-typed service calls where efficiency and contracts matter. GraphQL: When clients need very different shapes of the same graph and round trips are the pain.

questions.prompt: REST appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.

Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style) — The booking surface, where PUT/POST semantics and idempotency keys decide whether a double-tap books two seats.
Design a Webhook Delivery System — The contract you require of receivers — a URL, a 2xx and a timeout — which is the entire integration surface they implement.
questions.answer: REST carries different work in each: in Design a URL Shortener, the public creation and redirect surface, where a cacheable GET and a 301 are doing most of the work. in Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style), the booking surface, where PUT/POST semantics and idempotency keys decide whether a double-tap books two seats. in Design a Webhook Delivery System, the contract you require of receivers — a URL, a 2xx and a timeout — which is the entire integration surface they implement.

questions.prompt: Webhooks vs Cursor Pagination vs At-Least-Once Delivery — what decides between them?
points: Cursor Pagination — A polled cursor feed is far less machinery when near-real-time is not required.
At-Least-Once Delivery — The delivery guarantee webhooks provide — receivers must be idempotent.
Webhooks — Pushing events to a URL the customer registered, so their server learns about changes without polling yours.
questions.answer: Cursor Pagination: A polled cursor feed is far less machinery when near-real-time is not required. At-Least-Once Delivery: The delivery guarantee webhooks provide — receivers must be idempotent.

Result sets are large and clients page through them

Deep pages must stay as fast as shallow ones
questions.answer: Cursor Pagination. Returning a page plus an opaque cursor pointing at the last item, so the next page seeks rather than counting from the start. You reach for it when: Result sets are large and clients page through them; New items arrive while a client is paging — a feed, a log, a timeline; Deep pages must stay as fast as shallow ones.

Non-unique sort key causing rows at a boundary to be dropped

questions.prompt: Cursor Pagination vs Inverted Index / Search vs Server-Sent Events — what decides between them?
points: Inverted Index / Search — For ranked or faceted results, the engine's own paging semantics apply and deep paging is its own problem.
Server-Sent Events — If the client wants everything new as it happens, push beats repeated paging.
Cursor Pagination — Returning a page plus an opaque cursor pointing at the last item, so the next page seeks rather than counting from the start.
questions.answer: Inverted Index / Search: For ranked or faceted results, the engine's own paging semantics apply and deep paging is its own problem. Server-Sent Events: If the client wants everything new as it happens, push beats repeated paging.

questions.prompt: Cursor Pagination appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a News Feed — Cursor-based feed paging, so posts arriving mid-scroll do not shift the window and duplicate what the user just read.
Design a Chat System — Scrollback through message history, keyed on message id so a long thread pages backwards at constant cost.
Design a Proximity Service — Results page outward by distance band, so 'more places near me' does not rescan the whole radius.
Design a Search Engine — Result paging, where deep pages are expensive by construction because every shard must produce the full prefix.
questions.answer: Cursor Pagination carries different work in each: in Design a News Feed, cursor-based feed paging, so posts arriving mid-scroll do not shift the window and duplicate what the user just read. in Design a Chat System, scrollback through message history, keyed on message id so a long thread pages backwards at constant cost. in Design a Proximity Service, results page outward by distance band, so 'more places near me' does not rescan the whole radius. in Design a Search Engine, result paging, where deep pages are expensive by construction because every shard must produce the full prefix.
